# The Cybersecurity Talent Shortage: Calculating the Cost of the Empty Chair

Every day a Lead Application Security (AppSec) Engineer position remains open at a mid-market financial firm in Chicago, the business loses $10,310. 

This is not a theoretical loss. It is a compounding, daily tax calculated from direct contractor premiums, delayed product releases, and unmitigated risk exposure. Most hiring managers look at the cybersecurity talent shortage as an abstract market condition, a statistical cloud floating over the tech sector. They read reports about millions of unfilled roles globally and accept long hiring cycles as an unavoidable cost of doing business. 

By working backward from the actual cost of a vacancy, security leaders can change how they source, screen, and retain talent. The standard approach of waiting for a candidate who ticks every box is costing companies millions of dollars in quiet losses. To solve the talent shortage in your own organization, you must first understand the exact price of waiting.

## The Real Math Behind a Vacant Security Seat

To understand why traditional recruiting fails in security, we must break down the daily cost of an empty chair. Let us look at a typical mid-to-senior AppSec Engineer role in a major metropolitan area like Chicago or Charlotte, North Carolina. 

The market rate for this professional is roughly $175,000 in base salary. When we add benefits, payroll taxes, and overhead, the fully loaded cost of this employee is approximately $227,500 per year. This translates to $910 per business day. 

When this seat is empty, that $910 is not saved. Instead, it is replaced by several immediate expenses. First, the organization must cover the missing capacity. If you pull a senior developer or an infrastructure engineer to cover basic security reviews, you lose their primary output. If you bring in an external contract consultant to cover the gap, you will pay an average of $180 per hour. At eight hours a day, that is $1,440 per day, representing a daily premium of $530 over the salaried employee.

Second, product shipping delays occur. If a new software feature cannot clear its final security gate because there is no AppSec engineer to conduct the threat model or review the static analysis results, the release stalls. For a SaaS company with a projected pipeline, a 30-day delay on a major feature release can easily defer $150,000 in quarterly contract value. That adds $5,000 per day to the vacancy bill.

Third, there is the cost of increased risk. While difficult to quantify daily, insurance underwriters estimate that operating without dedicated application security monitoring increases the statistical probability of a successful breach. If a breach costs an average of $4.45 million, even a minor increase in probability adds hundreds of dollars in risk premium to your daily operations.

When you add the contractor premium, the delayed release pipeline, and the risk premium, the total cost of this single vacancy reaches $10,310 per day. With an average time-to-fill of 110 days for specialized security roles, a single open position can easily drain over $1.1 million in value before a candidate ever signs an offer letter.

## The Credential Inflation Trap

If the cost of an empty chair is so high, why do hiring managers allow positions to remain open for four to six months? The primary culprit is credential inflation, which is often driven by automated applicant tracking systems and outdated HR templates.

Many job descriptions for mid-level security roles require a Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP) credential. However, the CISSP exam requires a minimum of five years of direct, professional work experience in two or more of the eight domains of the CISSP CBK. By demanding a CISSP for an entry-to-mid-level role, hiring managers automatically disqualify thousands of capable professionals who have three years of intense, hands-on experience but lack the formal five-year milestone.

Similarly, requiring ten years of experience in cloud security is mathematically impossible for many modern toolsets. Technologies like Kubernetes and specific cloud native security platforms have only been widely adopted in enterprise environments for a fraction of that time. When HR filters require decade-long experience with modern tools, they create an artificial shortage.

This mismatch between written requirements and operational reality is where the talent shortage actually lives. The market does not lack people who can secure a network. It lacks people who can pass a screening process designed for a fictional candidate.

> **Benchmark:** According to data from the 2023 ISC2 Cybersecurity Workforce Study, the global cybersecurity workforce gap reached 4 million professionals, representing a 12.6% increase year-over-year, while 67% of organizations reported a shortage of cybersecurity staff needed to prevent security incidents.

## Sourcing from Adjacent Technical Pools

To bypass this structural bottleneck, successful hiring managers are looking outside traditional security pipelines. Some of the most capable security professionals do not start their careers in security. They transfer from adjacent technical fields.

A system administrator who has spent five years managing Active Directory and configuring network firewalls already understands the fundamentals of access control and network architecture. They do not need to be taught how a packet travels through a switch or how group policies work. They only need to be taught how to view these systems through an adversarial lens.

Likewise, software QA engineers make exceptional application security analysts. Their entire career is built on finding ways to break software. Teaching a QA engineer who already understands code logic and test automation how to spot a SQL injection or a cross-site scripting vulnerability is far easier than teaching a pure security theorist how to read enterprise Java code.

By targeting these adjacent pools, you can source candidates who are ready to perform on day one, even if they do not have a traditional security degree. This approach also allows you to bypass the intense salary competition for candidates who already hold standard security titles.

Using specialized sourcing partners like TaaSFlow can help identify these adjacent professionals who possess the raw technical capability but might be missed by generic keyword-matching algorithms. This targeted method reduces the average time-to-fill from 110 days to under 45 days, saving hundreds of thousands of dollars in vacancy costs.

## Practical Assessment Over Theoretical Certifications

Once you expand your sourcing pool to include adjacent talent, your screening process must change. If you rely on multiple-choice technical interviews, you will favor candidates who are good at memorizing definitions over those who can solve practical problems.

Instead of asking a candidate to define the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption, give them a realistic scenario. Show them a poorly configured cloud storage bucket or a snippet of code containing a hardcoded API key and ask them to identify the risk and explain how they would fix it.

This shift to practical assessment does three things:

First, it levels the playing field for self-taught professionals or those transitioning from other IT departments. A system administrator might not know the exact academic terminology for a specific attack vector, but they can spot an open port or an unpatched server instantly.

Second, it reduces hiring bias. When candidates are judged on their ability to find and fix vulnerabilities in a controlled environment, their pedigree, certifications, and previous job titles become secondary to their actual performance.

Third, it accelerates the hiring timeline. A structured, one-hour practical assessment provides more actionable data than three rounds of subjective technical interviews, allowing you to make offers faster and stop the daily financial drain of an unfilled position.

## Burnout and the Retention Tax

Solving the talent shortage is not just about bringing new people in. It is about keeping the ones you have. The security industry has one of the highest burnout rates in technology, with many professionals leaving their roles within two years due to stress and alert fatigue.

When a security team is understaffed, the burden falls on the remaining members. They must monitor alerts, respond to incidents, and conduct security reviews with fewer resources. This leads to a vicious cycle: an empty seat increases the workload on the remaining team, causing another member to burn out and resign, which doubles the vacancy cost for the business.

To break this cycle, security leaders must treat retention as a core component of their recruiting strategy. This means automating repetitive tasks like basic alert triage and vulnerability scanning to free up your team for more engaging work. It also means establishing clear boundaries for on-call rotations and ensuring that security analysts are not penalized for false positives.

If your team sees that you are actively working to reduce their operational burden, they are far more likely to stay, protecting you from the high cost of starting the hiring cycle all over again.

## What a Successful Security Hiring Process Looks Like

If you want to reduce your time-to-fill and secure capable talent in a competitive market, you need a structured, realistic hiring process. Here is what a successful sourcing and screening workflow looks like:

1. **Audit the Job Description:** Remove all non-essential certification requirements. If a task does not require a CISSP on day one, do not list it as a requirement.
2. **Target Adjacent Talent:** Search for system administrators, network engineers, and software QA professionals who have demonstrated an interest in security through personal projects or home labs.
3. **Implement a Practical Assessment:** Replace theoretical questions with a short, hands-on exercise that mirrors the actual work the candidate will do daily.
4. **Set a Strict Interview SLA:** Limit the hiring process to three stages (initial screen, practical assessment, team fit) and make a decision within 15 business days of the first contact.
5. **Offer Competitive, Transparent Compensation:** Do not try to lowball candidates in a high-demand market. A delayed hire to save $10,000 on base salary will cost you far more in daily vacancy expenses.
6. **Build a Clear Onboarding Plan:** Ensure the new hire has access to the tools, documentation, and peer support they need to become productive within their first 30 days.

By following this framework, organizations can build a resilient recruiting pipeline that relies on practical skill rather than credential checklists, allowing them to fill critical security roles before vacancy costs impact the bottom line.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why are entry-level security roles so difficult to find if there is a talent shortage?
The shortage is highly concentrated in mid-to-senior roles where independent decision-making is required. Many organizations are unwilling to invest in training entry-level talent, leading to an over-saturation of junior applicants competing for a tiny handful of associate roles, while senior roles remain vacant for months.

### Should we pay for our existing IT staff to get security certifications?
Yes, but with a clear plan. Funding certifications like the Security+ or GIAC certificates for your system administrators or developers is an excellent retention tool and a cost-effective way to build internal security talent, provided you offer them a clear path to transition into a dedicated security role within your organization.

### How can mid-market companies compete with enterprise tech salaries for security talent?
While salary is important, many security professionals are highly motivated by autonomy, modern toolsets, and the ability to make a visible impact. Highlight your flat organizational structure, minimize bureaucratic approval processes for security decisions, and offer flexible remote work options to attract top talent who are tired of enterprise red tape.

Every day a critical security seat remains empty, your organization pays a quiet, compounding tax in contractor premiums, delayed projects, and unmitigated risk.
